transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~53 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Rita Patel (CTO - SolaraHealth), Samir Khan (ML Eng), Jenna Li (PM)

Auto-generated Summary: (may be incomplete)
Maya provided an overview of Redwood's model catalog and use-case fit, Luis walked through compatibility matrices and benchmark slides, Solara asked about latency/cost tradeoffs and private deployment options. Next steps agreed: send pricing, share benchmark plan, start pilot.

Topics: Model catalog walkthrough, open model selection, benchmark methodology, quantization/compatibility notes, private deployment/SOC2/KMS questions.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood Inference, I'm the account exec. With me I've got Luis Ortega, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Rita: Hi Maya, thanks for setting this up. Doing well.
[00:07] Samir: Good afternoon, thanks.
[00:09] Jenna: Hi.
[00:12] Luis: Awesome. So today we'll run through the model catalog — how you pick open models, what the benchmarks look like, and when you'd choose hosted vs dedicated vs private. We'll also show the compatibility matrix and typical perf numbers.
[00:20] Maya: We also wanna learn about your success criteria and timeline, so we can tailor a pilot. Samir, can you give a quick 30-second on your current setup?
[00:28] Samir: Sure. We're running a mix — prod stuff uses a commercial API for summarization and triage, some internal tooling is on in-house models. Main constraints are latency under 400ms p50 for short prompts, and cost per 1000 tokens needs to be reasonable — finance will push back. Also we need HIPAA-adjacent controls, so data residency and key management are important.
[00:46] Maya: Got it, that's helpful. Luis, can you kick into the catalog demo?
[00:50] Luis: Yep. I'm sharing my screen — okay can you see the model catalog UI? (pause) Looks like the view is up. So top of the screen we have curated open models — we group them by capability and performance profile. For example we surface high-throughput 7B quantized variants, full-precision 13B candidates, and specialized rerankers/embedding models.
[01:15] Samir: Quick question — when you say quantized variants, are those things you produce or third-party builds?
[01:20] Luis: Good call. Mostly we're integrating community quantized builds but we also run internal validation and publish Redwood-verified profiles — latency, memory, and quality regression checks. The catalog shows the profile and a compatibility tag if it's good for KV cache, long context, or sharded execution.
[01:36] Rita: Can you show an example selection flow? Like we want low latency for 2-3 sentence prompts and high accuracy for clinical summarization.
[01:43] Luis: Sure. So I'd filter by target latency and then by evaluation suite — we run a standard clinical summarization eval for health customers. Picking a 7B q4 variant gives you really good latency — p50 often under 200ms on our dedicated pools — but there's a small quality delta vs a 13B fp16. We show that tradeoff inline with a redwood score that weights latency/cost/quality.
[02:05] Jenna: How are those numbers measured? Is that on load or single request?
[02:09] Luis: It's a mixture. We report single-request p50/p95 on our hosted infra, and also throughput with continuous batching on dedicated. For your pilot we can run the benchmark with your prompt set and report the same metrics under simulated traffic.
[02:23] Samir: That'd be great. Also, compatibility matrix — we have long documents occasionally, up to 8k tokens. Will the 7B quantized keep performance?
[02:32] Luis: For long contexts we usually recommend a 13B with better KV cache handling; some quantized 7Bs degrade after 4k tokens due to chunking and attention kernel fallbacks. The compatibility matrix shows which kernel path triggers for which seq len and hardware.
[02:47] Maya: Just to add, Redwood's runtime will auto-fallback to compatible model variants if the selected token length or hardware changes — so graceful degradation is built in.
[02:55] Rita: On the security side, what certifications do you have and how does KMS integrate? HIPAA is a big one for us.
[03:02] Maya: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II. For HIPAA, we support private deployments with customer-managed KMS, and our hosted offering has encryption at rest with customer-managed keys for enterprise tiers. We can share the security whitepaper.
[03:14] Samir: Do you have audit logs for token-level tracing? We need to show data lineage for compliance reviews.
[03:19] Luis: Yes, the Console provides token-level cost/latency breakdowns, and audit logs with S3-compatible export. For private deployments those logs stay in your VPC.
[03:29] [00:03:30] Samir: Good.
[03:31] Luis: Back to model selection — here's a demo of the benchmark tab. We have a set of synthetic workloads but the key is replacing with your prompts. You'll upload a CSV, we do warm-up runs, then report latency/throughput/cost per 1k tokens and a quality delta vs a reference model.
[03:49] Jenna: When you compute cost per 1k tokens, does that reflect quantization improvements? Like q4 vs fp16?
[03:55] Luis: Yes — cost per 1k is model+infra adjusted. Quantized variants often show a 2-3x lower token cost due to smaller memory and better batching, but again quality tradeoffs vary by task.
[04:08] Rita: About private deployments — if we go on-prem, how fast is onboarding?
[04:12] Maya: On-prem cadence depends on your infra. For VPC private deployments we have a control plane that sits outside but you can elect full air-gapped installs. Typical pilot for VPC is 2–6 weeks depending on approvals.
[04:22] Samir: Any limitations on GPUs or specific CUDA versions? We run a mix of A10s and H100s in prod.
[04:28] Luis: We support both; the runtime picks kernels optimized per hardware. We document exact CUDA/cudnn versions in the compatibility matrix. For H100 we get better throughput on fp16 and some special attention kernels.
[04:40] [00:04:45] Maya: We also often recommend a hybrid: start hosted to validate prompts quickly, then move to dedicated reserved capacity for predictability, and if you need compliance, transition to private.
[04:51] Rita: Can we see an example compatibility matrix row?
[04:54] Luis: Yep — here's a snippet: model name, quantization type, recommended sequence length, kernel path, verified libs (torch/TRITON/RTX). For example, OpenX-7B-q4 shows recommended seq len <= 4096, kernel path fallback to CPU attention beyond that.
[05:10] Samir: That fallback — does it cause large latency spikes?
[05:13] Luis: It can at p95; that's why we include automatic routing policies so we can route long-context requests to a 13B variant automatically.
[05:22] Jenna: For the pilot, would you run A/B against our current vendor?
[05:26] Maya: Absolutely, we can do an A/B with traffic split and side-by-side latency and quality dashboards.
[05:31] [00:05:35] Samir: Regarding benchmarks, what metrics do you include for quality? ROUGE? BLEU? Something clinical-specific?
[05:37] Luis: We support standard nlp metrics like ROUGE, BLEU, and also allow custom human evals. For clinical summarization we run entity recall and hallucination checks via a small annotator set. We can integrate your rubric.
[05:50] Rita: Pricing — ballpark for a pilot and then what committed capacity looks like?
[05:56] Maya: For a pilot we usually provide credits and a lightweight setup — pricing details I'd send in the follow-up. For Dedicated Reserved, commitments reduce per-token unit costs and we offer burst buckets. I'll send a tailored pricing sheet once we align on target throughput.
[06:10] Samir: One more technical — how do you handle model version pinning and rollbacks?
[06:14] Luis: Console supports semantic pinning and rollouts. You can pin runtime to exact model artifact and do canary rollouts. If quality regressions appear, automatic fallback policies will send traffic to the previous stable variant.
[06:25] Maya: Okay, we're approaching time. Final questions?
[06:28] Rita: Timelines — we want to run a 2-week pilot by early May. Can you support that?
[06:33] Maya: Yes, if we get your prompts and a small sample dataset by end of April we can aim for a May 4 kickoff.
[06:39] Samir: Sounds good. Luis, you'll own the benchmark plan?
[06:43] Luis: Yep I'll draft the checklist and compatibility matrix and we'll include instructions for the sample CSV.
[06:48] [00:06:50] Jenna: Also please include the data handling and KMS integration doc so we can route to Security for review.
[06:54] Maya: Will do.
[06:55] Maya: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the pricing and security docs, and Luis will share the benchmark plan. Any objections to me setting the pilot kickoff for May 4 provisional?
[07:04] Rita: No objections.
[07:06] Samir: Works for me.
[07:08] Maya: Awesome, thanks all.
[07:10] [00:07:10] End of call.

Notes / Observations:
- Customer is focused on latency and cost for short prompts but needs support for occasional long-context inputs (8k tokens).
- They prefer open models but are concerned about quantization-related quality regressions; Redwood suggested hybrid approach and automatic routing to larger variants when needed.
- Security and KMS/residency are gating factors; Redwood to provide SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
- Strong likelihood of pilot (2-week) followed by Dedicated reserved capacity if results are favorable.

Questions (captured):
- Can Redwood run benchmarks with Solara's prompt set? (Answer: yes)
- What exact CUDA/CUDNN versions are required for on-prem? (Luis will add to matrix)
- How are quality deltas measured for clinical summarization? (Custom metrics + small annotator pool)

- Link: Model catalog demo deck (Redwood internal slide link)
- Link: Benchmark checklist (to be shared by Luis)
